body.p: Claims 1-20 are pending in this application. In response to the Non-Final Office Action mailed February 26, 2024 (hereinafter "Office Action"), claims 1-20 have been canceled and new claims 21-42 have been added. Therefore, claims 21-42 remain pending. No new matter has been added. In view of the foregoing amendments and following comments, allowance of all the claims pending in the application is respectfully requested.

Applicant notes that a Preliminary Amendment with new claims was filed on February 13, 2024, before the issuance of the Non-Final Office Action mailed February 26, 2024. Applicant further notes the new claims filed in the Preliminary Amendment have not been entered and were not considered by the Examiner before the Non-Final Office Action was mailed. Additionally, a title change was submitted via a web corrected Application Data Sheet and excess claims fees were paid for the two claims over 20 submitted with the Preliminary Amendment on February 13, 2024. Applicant notes the title change and payment for excess claims fees were both entered. In response to the Non-Final Office Action mailed February 26, 2024, Applicant is re-submitting the new claims filed with the Preliminary Amendment filed on February 13, 2024 and is providing arguments in response to the Section 101 rejections.

Applicant has added new independent claims 21 and 32 directed towards a system and method for converting a bounded gameplay session to an unbounded gameplay session in a multiplayer video game for players of the multiplayer video game. The bounded gameplay session is configured to run until a predefined game objective is fulfilled or time has expired whereas the unbounded gameplay session is configured to run the game continuously. Based on a result of a query posed to a predetermined number of the players to determine if the bounded gameplay session should be converted to the unbounded gameplay session for all the players, perform the conversion and, thereafter, terminate the unbounded gameplay session only when no more of the players remain in the unbounded gameplay session. Support for independent claims 21 and 32 may be found in at least paragraph 79 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 22, 24, 33 and 35 are directed towards system and method for running the game continuously provided a minimum number of the players are in the unbounded gameplay session; and to not convert the bounded gameplay session to the unbounded gameplay session if the number of the players agreeing to said converting is below a predefined number. Support for dependent claims 22, 24, 33 and 35 may be found in at least paragraph 79 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 23 and 34 are directed towards system and method for determining whether to initiate the bounded gameplay session for all the players or the unbounded gameplay session for all the players and initiating the bounded gameplay session for all the players based on the determination. Support for dependent claims 23 and 34 may be found in at least paragraph 79 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 25-27 and 36-38 are directed towards systems and methods for using a matchmaking engine configured to create at least a first subset of players and a second subset of players from the players which may be based upon an election by at least one player of the players or on at least one of a skill level or a style of at least one player of the players. Support for dependent claims 25-27 and 36-38 may be found in at least paragraph 73 and 74 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 28 and 39 are directed towards system and method for using a scoring engine to generate scores for the players where the scores are not dependent on a total length of time the unbounded gameplay session has been played by one or more players of the players. Support for dependent claims 28 and 39 may be found in at least paragraph 86-88 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 29 and 40 are directed towards systems and methods for using a scoring engine to generate scores for the players wherein the scores are dependent on a total length of time the bounded gameplay session has been played by one or more players of the players. Support for dependent claims 29 and 40 may be found in at least paragraph 82-85 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.

New dependent claims 30, 31, 41 and 42 are directed towards system and method for using a game adjustment engine to monitor the unbounded gameplay session for determining a performance gap between the first subset of players and the second subset of players and generating and implementing an adjustment feature based on the performance gap. Support for
dependent claims 30, 31, 41 and 42 may be found in at least paragraph 99-100 of Applicant's Published US patent Application No. 20230001295A1.
REJECTIONS UNDER 35 USC SECTION 101

Claims 1-20 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is allegedly directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Examiner asserts the claims are directed to the abstract idea of mental processes and/ or certain methods of organizing human activity and allegedly do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception as discussed below.
Applicant submits its new claims are patentable under 35 U.S.C. Section 101 and are not directed to an abstract idea.

Assuming the amended claims are directed toward one of the statutory categories of invention, which they are, the amended claims must then be analyzed to determine whether they are directed to an abstract idea and if the elements in the amended claims amount to mere instructions applied using generic computer components. Here, the claims focus on a particular technological environment, namely multi-player video games-not just any game environment and are directed toward the execution and operation of multi-player video games-not to the manipulation of abstract data. The claims are actually directed towards converting a time bounded gameplay session which runs until a predefined game objective is fulfilled or time has expired to an unbounded gameplay session (in a multiplayer video game) which runs the game continuously, based on a result of a query posed to a predetermined number of the players. If the players show their interest, the time bound (bounded) game is converted to an unbounded gaming session thereby enhancing the gameplay experience of the players.

Since the Examiner states that the additional elements "a computer system and at least partially transmitted to a plurality of end user devices and wherein the computer system includes one or more processors executing a video game streaming application for generating and streaming the multi-player gameplay session" are mere instructions to apply the exception using generic computer components or software (that is, being well-understood, routine and conventional) and do not act as a transformative limitation, Applicant would like to bring to the Examiner's attention the Berkheimer memorandum (which follows the US Federal Circuit's opinion in Berkheimer v. HP case no. 2017-1437), and clarifies the second step of the Mayo/Alice test, and also revises the examination procedure for rejecting claims on that

basis. The memorandum states that the conclusion of whether an element is well-understood, routine and conventional must be based on a factual determination. The memo suggests that a claim recites "significantly more" unless proven otherwise, and states that an additional element is not well-understood, routine or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports such a rejection in writing. The memo makes clear that such a statement by the examiner will normally require a citation to be provided by the examiner.

Applicant submits that in McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco Games America, Inc. et al. (Fed. Cir. Sept. 13, 2016), the Federal Circuit held that claims directed to software for automatically animating lip synchronization and facial expressions of animated characters were not directed to an abstract idea under the first prong of the Alice test, and therefore recited patent-eligible subject matter. The Applicant's claims precisely meet the standards established in McRo v. Bandai Namco Games America wherein the Federal Circuit held that claim 1 was "directed to a patentable, technological improvement over the existing, manual 3-D animation techniques" and that claim 1 "uses the limited rules in a process specifically designed to achieve an improved technological result in conventional industry practice."

More specifically, Applicant's claims are directed toward an improvement "based on converting a bounded multiplayer video game session to an unbounded video game session based on querying a predefined number of players" and that "the claimed alteration of game playing experience, not the implementation of a general purpose computer, improved existing technology", akin to the claims in McRO. Examiner's position then really boils down to a sole differentiator-is converting a timed game to an unbounded gaming session based on responses received from players in a multi-player gaming session in order to improve game playing experience for the players - a computer-related technology, as much as lip sync animation?

Applicant submits that there is nothing in the existing patent rules or legal precedent that would warrant categorizing the above said claimed steps for providing an advantage in the game to those players that respond favorably to a query for converting a timed game to an unbounded game that runs continuously till the players play the game, as a non-computer- related technology. Stating that the Applicant's claimed steps is an activity that could be done manually by humans ignores the facts underlying the decision in McRO. The McRO patent aimed to automate a 3-D animator's tasks-tasks that were once done manually-by determining when to set keyframes and setting those keyframes. This automation is accomplished through rules that are applied to the timed transcript to determine the morph weight outputs. There is no conceptual difference between the automation of a manual human

task in animation using a novel rule set and the conversion of a timed game to an unbounded gaming session based on data received from players in a multi-player gaming session in order to improve game playing experience for the players.

Applicant would like to submit that the pending claims are not directed to mental activity/the grouping or organization of human activity outside of a technical context. Unlike previous decisions dealing with the "organization of human activity", computers are not being used incidentally to organize or direct humans in a non-technical context. Rather, every aspect of human interaction is in the context of a technical computing world-converting a time bound game to an unbounded game in multiplayer video games -which requires an improvement in key technology related to multi-player video games.

Even assuming arguendo that Applicant's claims are directed to an abstract idea (which, at least for the reasons above, they are not), the claimed combination of features of Applicant's claims would meaningfully limit the application of the purported abstract idea in order to solve a problem faced within multi-player video games and/or would transform the purported abstract idea into a particular practical application of modulating gameplay experience of one or more players. In particular, Applicant's claims satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. Section 101 at least for the reasons that the claims of DDR Holdings and BASCOM were held to satisfy the requirements of 35 USC Section 101.

Applicant submits that Applicant's claims, similar to the claim at issue in DDR Holdings "...do[es] not recite a mathematical algorithm. Nor do[es] [it] recite a fundamental economic or longstanding commercial practice. Although the claims address a challenge directed towards enhancing player experience, it is a challenge particular to the technical field of multi-player video games." DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P., 773 F.3d 1245, 1257 (Fed. Cir. 2014). Applicant further submits that Applicant's claims, similar to the claim at issue in BASCOM, "...do[es] not merely recite the abstract idea of [displaying and manipulating data] with the requirement to perform it on a computer system, or to perform it on a set of generic computer components...[n]or do the claims preempt all ways of [displaying and manipulating data]; rather, they recite a specific, discrete implementation of [converting a time bound gameplay session which runs until a predefined game objective is fulfilled or time has expired to an unbounded gameplay session (in a multiplayer video game) which runs the game continuously, based on a result of a query posed to a predetermined number of the players, thereby enhancing the gameplay experience of the players]." BASCOM Global Internet Services, Inc. v.A T&TMobility LLC (Appeal No. 2015-1763, Fed. Cir. 2016). Therefore, as in

DDR Holdings and BASCOM, Applicant's claimed combination of the additional limitations would meaningfully limit the application of the purported abstract idea in order to solve a tangible, practical, real world problem.

In the interest of clarity and brevity, Applicant may not have addressed every assertion made in the Office Action. Applicant's silence regarding any such assertion does not constitute any admission or acquiescence. Applicant reserves all rights not exercised in connection with this response, such as the right to challenge or rebut any tacit or explicit characterization of any reference or of any of the present claims, the right to challenge or rebut any asserted factual or legal basis of any of the rejections, the right to swear behind any cited reference such as provided under 37 C.F.R. § 1.131 or otherwise, or the right to assert co-ownership of any cited reference. Applicant does not admit that any of the cited references or any other references of record is relevant to the present claims, or that they constitute prior art. To the extent that any rejection or assertion is based upon the Examiner's personal knowledge, rather than any objective evidence of record as manifested by a cited prior art reference, Applicant timely objects to such reliance on Official Notice, and reserves all rights to request that the Examiner provide a reference or affidavit in support of such assertion, as required by MPEP § 2144.03. Applicant reserves all rights to pursue any cancelled claims in a subsequent patent application claiming the benefit of priority of the present patent application, and to request rejoinder of any withdrawn claim, as required by MPEP § 821.04.
Respectfully submitted,
